```
# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The PriceFeed.sol was marked OOS but I believe this to be a valid issue. If the chainlink feed fails which is does from time to time, the Tellor price feed takes over no matter what the delta is compared to the chainlink price. 2.. Reports an inflated price.
```

issues.title: `CommunityIssuance` doesn't check the return value of `OathToken.transferFrom()` and `OathToken.transfer()`
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/73687f32b934c9d697b97745356cdf8a1f264955/Ethos-Core/contracts/LQTY/CommunityIssuance.sol#L103

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `CommunityIssuance.fund()` calls `OathToken.transferFrom()` but doesn't check the return value, which indicates whether the transfer succeeded or failed. Similarly, the function `CommunityIssuance.sendOath()` calls `OathToken.transfer()` but doesn't check the return value, which indicates whether the transfer succeeded or failed.

Because of these two issues, LQTY gains may not be send to users (by the `StabilityPool`), if for example the owner didn't set a correct allowance before initially calling `CommunityIssuance.fund()`.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Check the return value.

issues.title: ReaperVaultERC4626.sol is not EIP-4626 compliant
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/73687f32b934c9d697b97745356cdf8a1f264955/Ethos-Vault/contracts/ReaperVaultERC4626.sol#L12-L276


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Other protocols integrated with Ethos Reserve may mistakenly assume that its function complies with EIP-4626. Therefore, this may lead to integration issues in the future, which could result in various problems for both parties.

## Proof of Concept
All official EIP-4626 requirements can be found on it's https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626#methods official page. Non-compliant functions are listed below along with the reason they are not compliant:

The following functions are missing but should be present:

mint(uint256, address) returns (uint256)
redeem(uint256, address, address) returns (uint256)
The following functions are non-compliant because they don't account for withdraw and deposit locking:

-maxDeposit
-maxMint
-maxWithdraw
-maxRedeem

All of the above functions should return 0 when their respective functions are disabled (i.e. maxDeposit should return 0 when deposits are disabled)

previewDeposit is not compliant because it must account for fees which it does not

totalAssets is not compliant because it does not always return the underlying managed by the vault because it fails to include the assets paid out during a depeg or the end of the epoch.
## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
All functions listed above should be modified to meet the specifications of EIP-4626

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
ReaperStrategyGranarySupplyOnly calls function __ReaperBaseStrategy_init() from ReaperBaseStrategyv4, 
but ReaperBaseStrategyv4 is not Initializable. If the __ReaperBaseStrategy_init function is not called during contract initialization, it can cause critical issues as the state variables initialized in this function won't be set properly. This can lead to unexpected behavior and vulnerabilities such as reentrancy, funds being stuck in the contract, or even complete loss of funds.

For example, if "want" is not initialized properly, the contract may not be able to interact with the expected token and may result in users' funds being locked in the contract indefinitely. 
Similarly, if roles are not initialized properly, it can result in unauthorized access to sensitive functions or funds.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Recommended steps: Add Initializable to contract declaration.

```
abstract contract ReaperBaseStrategyv4 is
    ReaperAccessControl,
    IStrategy,
    UUPSUpgradeable,
    AccessControlEnumerableUpgradeable,
    "Initializable"
```

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Core/contracts/LQTY/LQTYStaking.sol#L104


# Vulnerability details

In the LQTY smart contract, the stake() and unstake() functions are used to add or remove a certain amount of LQTY tokens from a user's stake, respectively. Both functions are designed to update the user's stake and the total amount of LQTY staked while allowing users to withdraw any accumulated gains in collateral and LUSD tokens.

The unstake() function is vulnerable to reentrancy attacks. This means that a malicious attacker could call the unstake() function and then call a fallback function on a malicious contract that could immediately call the unstake() function again before the initial call is completed, leading to a reentrancy attack. 

To mitigate this vulnerability, the following should be considered:

-Use a mutex to prevent multiple simultaneous calls to the unstake() function.

-Implement the checks-effects-interactions pattern, where all checks are performed before any external interactions are made. This will ensure that the state of the contract is updated before any external calls are made, preventing any potential reentrancy attacks.

-Limit the amount of LQTY tokens that can be unstaked at any given time. This will limit the potential damage caused by a reentrancy attack and allow for easier recovery in the event of an attack.

issues.title: ActivePool.sol – Re-entrancy risk on _rebalance function
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Core/contracts/ActivePool.sol#L239


# Vulnerability details

The `_rebalance` function is vulnerable to a reentrancy attack. Specifically, an external callee can take over the control flow of the function by calling back into the `ActivePool` contract via a method that triggers the `_rebalance` function again before it completes the execution of its current invocation. If this happens, the attacker can execute additional logic in the context of the partially executed `_rebalance` function, bypass some checks and extract additional funds. 

Since the `_rebalance` function updates and reclaims funds from external contracts such as `yieldGenerator` contract and LQTY's `StabilityPool` contract, reentrancy attacks can enable attackers to steal additional funds than they are entitled to. For example, an attacker can repeatedly withdraw their profits from the `yieldGenerator` during the attack and bypass the check that examines the performance fees. 

Solution: To mitigate this vulnerability, the `_rebalance` function should be designed as a non-reentrant function to ensure that it completes the execution of its current invocation before allowing a new one to begin. One way to achieve this is by using the OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard` library or a similar technique.

Additionally, the withdrawFromSP function could implement a reentrancy guard to prevent multiple calls to the same function during execution.

```solidity
# Vulnerability details

## Description
There are many places in the code where token transfers are in the middle of a function (more specifically, both after and before state changes). It is very important not to pass control to untrusted code in these calls, as they could potentially re-enter and cause havoc, since the system is at present in a "dirty state" (i.e. a yet-uncommitted temporary state where important system invariants might not hold).

## Exploit scenario
Mallory is a malicious hacker. She interacts with the system in such a way that she is at either the receiving or sending end of a transfer of a token with callback support. Since system invariants don't hold at this time, she is able to exploit the situation to make a profit, potentially at the expense of other users.

## Recommendation
Review every token that the system interacts with to ensure it does not hand control to untrusted code, in particular callback tokens. Callback tokens that are also compliant with ERC20 include ERC223 and 777. ERC721 and 1155 have slightly different semantics and interface, but also allow for callbacks. Additionally:

- ensure protocol tokens (Ern and Oath) do not allow callbacks. This was the cause of the Siren hack [link](https://medium.com/siren/siren-incident-report-264e57f16d7).
- ensure the user may not submit a token that is untrusted. This was the precipitate of the Origin Dollar hack [link](https://peckshield.medium.com/origin-dollar-incident-root-cause-analysis-f27e11988c90).

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When a user wants to earn collateral gains, typically they need to stake their funds. However, there is a way to earn collateral gains without staking funds by front-running the increaseF_Collateral function call.

By front-running, the user is able to anticipate a transaction before it is confirmed on the blockchain by placing their own transaction ahead of it. By doing this, the user can gain collateral without staking their funds.

It's important to note that the amount of time the user stakes is not a factor in their ability to earn collateral gains through front-running. This is because front-running allows the user to bypass the need for staking entirely.

However, timing is crucial when front-running. If the user executes the front-running at the correct time, they can earn collateral gains without having to stake their funds. But if they mistime the front-running, they could potentially lose money.

## Proof of Concept
Flow:
1. User rebalances with the `manualRebalance` function.
2. This internally calls `increaseF_Collateral`
3. Malicious actor frontrun this request and call the `stake` function with a big `_LQTYamount` [X]
4. This 3) request will run first, and increases the attacker stakes
5. Owner request to rebalance then
6. -> This increases the collateral `F_Collateral[_collateral]`
7. Attacker can directly call the `unstake` function.
8. `_sendCollGainToUser` will then send the gains to the Malicious actor balance ( = [X] ).

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
When calculating gains, it's important to take into account the duration for which the user has staked their funds before rewarding them for that amount.
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Vault/contracts/ReaperVaultV2.sol#L366


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When withdrawing from a vault, the user passes the amount of shares to be burnt, and in return the user receives the corresponding assets as follows:
```sh
value = (_freeFunds() * _shares) / totalSupply();
```

If there is not enough balance in the vault, then it withdraws from strategies in the order they were added in `withdrawalQueue`. However, in case the strategies don't have enough balance, the vault burns all user's shares even though s/he hasn't received all of the corresponding assets for it.

In other words, if the user should receive **Y** tokens when passing **X** shares and the issue occurs, then **X** shares will be burnt even though the user receives less than **Y** which is not fair.



## Proof of Concept

Let's break down `_withdraw`'s flow:

1. Calculate how many tokens the user should receive
```sh
   value = (_freeFunds() * _shares) / totalSupply();
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Vault/contracts/ReaperVaultV2.sol#L365

2. Burn the shares
```sh
   _burn(_owner, _shares);
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Vault/contracts/ReaperVaultV2.sol#L366

3. Assume there’s not enough fund in the vault then it will loop through `withdrawalQueue` and withdraw what's required to cover the gap.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Vault/contracts/ReaperVaultV2.sol#L372-L397

4. Assume the tokens the user should receive is still lower than the balance then update it to the balance

```sh
vaultBalance = token.balanceOf(address(this));
```

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Vault/contracts/ReaperStrategyGranarySupplyOnly.sol#L62-L72


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The difference between a **constructor** and a regular function is that Solidity takes care of automatically invoking the constructors of all ancestors of a contract. "When writing an initializer, you need to take special care to manually call the initializers of all parent contracts". Due to a requirement of the proxy-based upgradeability system, no constructors can be used in upgradeable contracts. Therefore, when the initializers in parent contracts aren't manually called, they are never automatically invoked by solidity.
As a result, **ReaperStrategyGranarySupplyOnly.sol** never has access to variables initialized in **ReaperBaseStrategyv4.sol** initializer function. 
Refer to OpenZeppelin's documentation on upgradeable contracts: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/upgrades-plugins/1.x/writing-upgradeable#initializers

## Proof of Concept
The **ReaperStrategyGranarySupplyOnly.sol** inherits the **ReaperBaseStrategyv4.sol** contract but the initializer of the **ReaperBaseStrategyv4.sol** isn't invoked in the **ReaperStrategyGranarySupplyOnly.sol**. This leads to the **strategies** in the **ReaperStrategyGranarySupplyOnly.sol** contract never being initialized.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Invoke the initializer function of **ReaperBaseStrategyv4.sol** in the initializer of its child contract, **ReaperStrategyGranarySupplyOnly.sol**. For example:
```
contract MyContract is BaseContract {
    uint256 public x;

    function initialize(uint256 _x) public initializer {
        BaseContract.initialize(); // Do not forget this call!
        x = _x;
    }
}
```

```
## Impact
Attacker can prevent depositors from depositing on the Reaper Vault V2

## Proof of Concept
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
According to discussion with the team, liquidations of the last Trove is prevented to mimic behavior of Liquity. It is expected that 1) the only ERN in circulation would be ERN belonging to that trove, and 2) there are no other troves to redistribute the debt to. However, this is not the case in Reserve. ERN can be minted from other collateral types and deposited into the Stability Pool, which can offset an entire Trove debt.

When the system is in recovery mode and a user calls `TroveManager.liquidate()`, the sequence attempts to liquidate a user provided number of Troves. The function that gets subsequently called is `_liquidateRecoveryMode`. This [check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/73687f32b934c9d697b97745356cdf8a1f264955/Ethos-Core/contracts/TroveManager.sol#L372) skips the Trove if there is 1 or fewer Troves remaining. This is problematic because the last Trove is essentially immune from liquidations, regardless of what it's ICR is.  

## Proof of Concept
Consider that there are 2 Trove types: BTC and ETH
- Alice opens a BTC trove and mints 5000 ERN.
- Alice deposits all her ERN into StabilityPool.
- Bob and Carol both open and mint smaller amounts of ERN (100 and 100, respectively) to ETH Troves. Their ICR are healthy (>= 150%).
- A collapse of ETH price happens and causes their ICR to plummet enough to get [offset by the Stability Pool](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/73687f32b934c9d697b97745356cdf8a1f264955/Ethos-Core/contracts/TroveManager.sol#L415).
- Liquidator calls liquidate
- Carol gets liquidated (Stability Pool picks offsets all of Carol's debt), but Bob does not, since he's the last trove remaining.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Consider removing the last trove check for liquidations

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Core/contracts/LUSDToken.sol#L282


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

- **LUSDToken** has a `permit` function allowing approvals using off-chain signatures. The signed message includes a **nonce** to prevent a transaction replay and a **deadline** to set some validity period of the signature. Whenever, a signature is utilized, the nonce is increased to allow the owner to off-chain sign further approvals. However, in case any signature expired before utilizing it, the transaction will always revert and the nonce will never increase.
This leads to:
	1. The function permit is no longer usable with new nonces for the relevant owner.
	2. The owner can only sign a new message with the nonce that was already used in the expired signature which is not a good practice since the purpose of nonce is to prevent replays.




## Proof of Concept

Have a look at the following scenario:

1. Bob signed a message with:
nonce = 1 and a deadline = tomorrow
2. Bob's current nonce is 1
3. Two days passed.

```sh
require(deadline >= now, 'LUSD: expired deadline');
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-02-ethos/blob/main/Ethos-Core/contracts/LUSDToken.sol#L282

Manual analysis
